summary:
We developed TrendScope, an interactive platform that shows what is changing in NASA Earth observation data, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users pick a variable (vegetation greenness, NDVI, from MOD13Q1 v061 at 250 m, or day/night land surface temperature from MOD11C3 v061 at 0.05°) and a place (the Nile Delta and its governorates, other world regions, any coordinates via NASA POWER, a drawn area, or their own GeoJSON or CSV, for example exported from NASA AppEEARS).

We validated the tool with an El-Andalos (New Cairo) case study built from AppEEARS data.

TrendScope directly answers the challenge's core questions: what is changing, where it varies spatially, how much it shifts, and whether changes are statistically significant. Its engine computes Hirsch-Slack Seasonal Mann-Kendall tests, deseasonalized Theil-Sen slopes with 95% confidence intervals, Pettitt regime-shift tests, and NDVI–LST thermal-canopy coupling, paired with account-based saved cases (My Cases), a strictly metrics-grounded AI Scientist, and one-click scientific PDF reports.

This is important because environmental shifts are rarely uniform globally—regional greening, drought stress, and urban or agricultural warming vanish inside global averages without rigorous, transparent local trend detection.
details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

TrendScope is an end-to-end Earth observation and statistical trend-detection web platform built for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. It turns multi-decadal NASA satellite observations into interactive visual and statistical evidence, answering four core scientific questions for any chosen region or coordinate on Earth:

1. What is changing?

Track Vegetation Cover (NDVI from NASA Terra MODIS `MOD13Q1.061` at 250 m resolution) and Daytime/Nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST from MODIS `MOD11C3.061` at 0.05° CMG) from 2000 to 2024—or upload custom GeoJSON polygons and NASA AppEEARS Statistics CSV tables.

2. Where is it changing?
Inspect curated global trend signals and regional benchmarks (Global Land Mean, Amazon Basin, Sahel, California Central Valley, and Nile Delta basins) or click any coordinate on Earth via interactive MapLibre GIS with live NASA POWER agroclimatology queries.

3. How much is it changing?

For each analysis TrendScope reports the size of the change as a deseasonalized Theil-Sen slope per decade with a 95% confidence interval, the total change over the selected period (absolute and as a percentage), and a seasonal breakdown (DJF, MAM, JJA, SON) showing whether the change is concentrated in one part of the year. For example, in our El-Andalos case study, greenness (NDVI) rose by about +0.012 per decade (95% CI roughly 0.010 to 0.013) [from the 300-month series].

4. Is it statistically significant?

Apply Hirsch–Slack Seasonal Mann-Kendall testing (`period=12`) to control for seasonal crop/solar cycles and Pettitt change-point tests to detect abrupt regime shifts, explicitly comparing local trends against global baselines.

Users can also sign in to manage saved investigations in "My Cases", query a strictly evidence-grounded  "AI Scientist", and export one-click publication-ready "PDF scientific dossiers" complete with DOIs, limitations, and methodology citations.

How does it work?

• Data ingestion. A FastAPI backend combines calibrated NASA Terra MODIS products (MOD13Q1 v061 and MOD11C3 v061), live NASA POWER point retrievals, and NASA AppEEARS CSV uploads (QA, angle and metadata fields are filtered out automatically to isolate the main scientific variable).

• Statistical engine. Environmental time series are often non-normal and strongly seasonal, so TrendScope uses non-parametric tests: the seasonal Mann-Kendall test (Hirsch-Slack, period = 12), deseasonalized Theil-Sen slopes, and the Pettitt change-point test, plus regional-versus-global divergence tests.

• Interface and grounded AI. A React + TypeScript interface shows MapLibre GL maps and Plotly.js time-series charts with trend lines and confidence bands. An AI Scientist (Gemini 2.5 Flash, with a deterministic fallback) writes its explanation from the computed backend metrics only, and ReportLab compiles statistics, interpretation and data limitations into PDF reports.

• Validation. We checked the pipeline with an AppEEARS case study in El-Andalos, New Cairo, analysing the data ourselves and comparing with the tool.

What benefits does it have?

• Eliminates global-average blind spots. Exposes regional warming, drought stress, and vegetation shifts that are hidden when looking only at global means.

• Scientific rigor made accessible. Automates proper seasonality control (seasonal Mann-Kendall), pixel-reliability awareness, and 95% uncertainty bounds in seconds, without requiring researchers, students, or policymakers to write statistical pipelines from scratch.

• Reproducibility and transparency. Every metric carries dataset DOIs, coordinate bounds, clear statistical significance flags (p < 0.05 vs. p ≥ 0.05), and dataset limitations, plus user-saved investigations (My Cases) and shareable PDF dossiers.

 What Do We Hope to Achieve?

We want students and curious members of the public to become data detectives: to find out what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant or could be chance. We hope the tool makes trend analysis of NASA data accessible, shows clearly what a “significant” trend does and does not mean (it is not proof of cause, and satellite artifacts can create false trends), and lets anyone test their own place or dataset.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

• Backend and scientific computing: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, xarray, rasterio, rioxarray, geopandas, Shapely, earthaccess, pystac-client, httpx, ReportLab (PDF generation), pytest.

• Frontend and geospatial visualization: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, React Query, React Router, i18next (multilingual support), MapLibre GL JS, Turf.js, Plotly.js, Framer Motion, Lucide React.

• NASA data and external services: NASA Terra MODIS (MOD13Q1 v061, MOD11C3 v061), NASA POWER API, NASA EOSDIS Earthdata / CMR / OPeNDAP, NASA AppEEARS CSV compatibility, NASA GISTEMP v4 reference baseline, NASA Visible Earth Blue Marble, MapTiler and CARTO Dark Matter basemaps, and Google Gemini API (gemini-2.5-flash).

NOTE: To check TrendScope, we extracted NASA MODIS Terra data (MOD13A3 NDVI and MOD11A2 land surface temperature, 1 km) for one polygon of about 12 pixels in El-Andalos through NASA AppEEARS, analysed it ourselves, and compared the results with the tool [: both found the same direction and significance, with slopes within about 8%].

Greenness (NDVI) rose by about +0.012 per decade (p < 0.0001), from roughly 0.08 to 0.12, but stays low (near barren ground); the rise is also significant for 2001–2019 alone.

Night-time temperature rose by about +1.7 to +2.1 °C per decade (p < 0.0001).

Daytime temperature fell by about 1.2 °C per decade, but the pre-2020 decrease is much smaller (−0.3 to −0.4 °C) and method-dependent. Part of the decline is probably an artifact of Terra crossing earlier in the morning since 2020. The whole Nile Delta shows no significant daytime trend over 2000–2024
